# In Praise of Middles

There is a stretch of every long drive—say, hour four of a nine-hour trip—when the journey loses both of its stories at once. The story of leaving is finished: the packing is done, the goodbyes said, the first hundred miles of novelties catalogued. But the story of arriving hasn't begun; the destination is still an abstraction, a pin on a map. What remains is a band of hours with no narrative charge at all. The billboards repeat. The radio thins out into static and syndication. You pass a water tower shaped like a soup can, and then thirty more minutes of nothing, and you realize that no photograph will ever be taken in this part of the trip. This stretch has no genre. It is simply the middle, and almost nothing in our culture has been built to honor it.

Consider how thoroughly we ritualize the edges of things. We commemorate firsts obsessively: first steps photographed, first days of school documented beside the front door, first kisses replayed, premiers and ribbon-cuttings and launch parties. We ritualize endings with equal devotion: graduations, retirement parties, funerals, farewell tours, series finales. Walk down a greeting-card aisle sometime and notice the economy of edges—whole racks of Congratulations and whole racks of Sympathy. There is a card for starting chemo and a card for ringing the bell. There is no card that says *Happy Seventh Month of Physical Therapy*. Nobody throws a party for reaching Wednesday. Nobody frames the picture taken on day 118 of anything.

This bias makes a certain sense. Beginnings are saturated with promise; they brim with unwritten possibility, and psychologists have found that much of the happiness of a vacation is savored before the plane ever leaves the gate. Endings deliver meaning: they let us see the shape of a thing, release the tension, apply the interpretation. Story itself demands edges. A beginning announces, an ending resolves, and our minds, which are compulsive storytellers, gravitate toward whatever feeds the plot.

But there is a stranger mechanism underneath the cultural one, and it lives inside each of us. Psychologists studying how we remember experiences have found something disarmingly simple: we do not remember durations. Asked how painful a medical procedure was, people report an average of the worst moment and the final moments—and essentially ignore how long the whole thing lasted. This holds for colonoscopies and cold-water experiments and, presumably, for Tuesday afternoons. Researchers call it duration neglect, and Daniel Kahneman built part of his career on its implications, arguing that each of us is inhabited by two selves. The experiencing self lives moment to moment, inside the actual duration of a life. The remembering self keeps the highlights reel: the peaks, the finales, little else. When the two selves disagree about whether a life went well, the remembering self usually wins the argument, because it is the one holding the pen.

Look closely at what this means. The remembering self is a ruthless editor: it preserves the trailer and burns the footage. And the footage—the vast, undifferentiated middle of things—is not a small portion of a life to be trimmed for pacing. It is nearly the whole film. Most of a marriage consists of Tuesday evenings. Most of parenthood consists of school pickups, snack negotiations, and fevers that break at 2 a.m. Most of a friendship is maintained through check-ins so unremarkable neither party could describe them a week later. If the remembering self discards middles, then our autobiographies systematically erase most of our lives, keeping the hinges and discarding the door.

And yet middles are where everything actually gets made. Anyone who has learned a difficult skill knows the geography of the plateau—that flat country between ascents where practice continues but measurable progress vanishes. It is the loneliest phase of learning, because we carry inside us a fantasy graph in which improvement rises smoothly forever, and against that fantasy the plateau registers as failure. In reality the plateau is consolidation: the quiet work of stitching knowledge into reflex, the fingers learning what the mind believed it had already taught. Nearly every skill worth having was built during weeks in which the builder felt stuck. The stuckness was the construction.

Love has its plateaus too. A wedding occupies an afternoon; a marriage is twenty thousand Tuesday nights, most of them fine, none of them instagrammable. The romantic myth teaches us to evaluate relationships by their edges—the falling-in and, if it comes to it, the falling-apart—and so we misread the long level middle as stagnation, when it may in fact be the achievement itself. Stability rarely signals. It just persists, without announcements, doing the load-bearing work of a life.

Artists understand all this, because artists collide with the middle professionally. Ask any novelist about the swampy stretch two-thirds through a draft, when the premise has been spent and the ending not yet sighted. Screenwriters speak of page sixty the way sailors speak of a particular reef: so many scripts die there that the territory has a name—the muddy middle. The conventions of storytelling were invented largely as technology for dragging audiences through it: introduce complications, raise stakes, break the hero's heart around minute ninety.

Music handles the problem with unusual honesty. In sonata form, after the exposition states its melodies and before the recapitulation restores order, there is the development section—and the development section is where the composer deliberately takes those beautiful themes apart. Fragmentation, modulation, keys sliding sideways; tension sustained without resolution, sometimes for minutes. It is the hardest passage to compose and, for listeners who learn to hear it, often the most gripping, because nothing is being presented and everything is being transformed. The development section is the sonata's middle, and composers stopped apologizing for it centuries ago. So did distance runners, who know that marathons are decided not at the electric start nor on the finishing straightaway but in the featureless middle miles, where starting-line adrenaline and finish-line hope are both spent and what remains is pacing, fueling, and the plain refusal to stop. Runners even have a name for the physiological ambush that arrives around mile eighteen or twenty, when the body's easy sugar runs out: hitting the wall. The wall is a middle phenomenon. It stands in every one.

Perhaps nowhere is the middle more haunted than in a human life itself. Large surveys across dozens of countries keep finding a similar curve when they track wellbeing across the lifespan: happiness tends to be high in youth, declines gradually through the thirties and forties, bottoms out somewhere around fifty, and then—to almost everyone's surprise—rises again, often surpassing the levels of early adulthood. The causes debated are fascinating, but the shape alone tells a story: life is a valley with a middle at the bottom of it. Scholars of aging suggest one explanation in particular that rings true. Early adulthood is defined by an ocean of open possibility—all the people you might become, all the lives you might yet lead. By middle age, the ocean has been draining steadily. Doors have swung shut, some gently, some slammed. And this sounds like pure loss until you notice what else closes: the exhausting obligation to keep every door propped open. Each shut door is also a stopped leak. There is a specific relief in a decision finally made permanent, in mourned possibilities becoming simply the neighbors of a chosen life rather than its indictments.

Dante located himself with terrible precision on this curve. His great poem opens—not, please notice, at a birth or a death, but *nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita*: midway upon the journey of our life. He finds himself awake in a dark wood, the straightforward path lost, and it is exactly there, in the unfashionable middle of a mismanaged life, that his vision begins. The Comedy is a poem about being stranded in the middle and discovering that the middle, walked through patiently, becomes a road. Dante wrote it in exile—a man in the middle of everything, denied both the city he began in and any clear place to end—and he turned that condition into a map the rest of us still consult seven centuries later. Whatever else the poem teaches, it teaches this: the fact that nothing has hardened into plot yet is precisely what leaves room for transformation. Middles are unfinished, and the unfinished is the only material change has ever worked with.

It occurs to me, pushing further, that the middle may be less a stretch of time than a kind of social position—which is why we treat it as an insult. Look how many middles name the overlooked: the middle child, the middle seat, middle management, middle school, middling reviews damning with faint praise. Our very atlas is organized around a middle that matters mainly as passage—the Mediterranean, the middle of the lands, a sea prized for the shores it connects. Whole regions and eras and classes get defined as corridors between the places where history supposedly happens. Meanwhile, civilization's real continuity depends on work that is structurally middle-shaped: the plumber repairing pipes no one thinks about until they fail, the teacher in week twelve of a semester, the nurse on a Tuesday night shift, the crews who keep the electrical grid humming through decades of unremarkable weather. Parades are thrown for product launches and mergers; nobody holds a ceremony for a decade of preventive maintenance. Yet strip away the middle-workers—the maintainers, the carriers of water in both senses—and every glamorous beginning and every tearful ending evaporates, because there would be no functioning world for either one to happen in.

Here, though, is the strangest twist, the one I keep circling back to: from the inside, the middle cannot actually be experienced as a middle. That designation exists only on maps drawn afterward, by remembering selves tracing routes. While you are in it—this hour, this errand, this ordinary evening—it is not the middle of anything. It is simply now, the only location consciousness has ever occupied. Try dividing a flowing river into thirds; you will need to stand on the bank to do it, and standing on the bank means getting out of the water. Every attempt to feel the middle from within dissolves into pure presence. In this sense the middle is not a thing among other things. It is the native habitat of experience, and the edges—those celebrated, ceremonial shores—are features of retrospection, cartography applied to country that never held still long enough to survey.

Which reframes everything. If the middle cannot be entered or exited, then there is no waiting to be done before a life qualifies as underway. The art of loving a life cannot consist of arranging for better edges, since the edges belong to memory anyway and memory will handle them without consultation. The art must consist of something harder and quieter: granting unspectacular nows their full weight while they are happening, on their own terms rather than as corridors. Duration neglect is not destiny. It can be resisted, a little, by whoever troubles to notice hour four of the drive while it is still hour four.

Because here is the last consoling joke of it: arrival changes nothing essential. The exit ramp appears, the city resolves out of haze, and within an hour the visit will have become another sequence unfolding—whose own center of gravity, statistically, will be found not at its welcome dinner or its farewell breakfast but somewhere in the level middle of it, say Thursday at noon, quiet, unmapped, holding everything. Beginnings look like gifts and endings look like meanings, but a life is conducted almost entirely in the space between, the way a symphony's heart beats in its developments, the way a wall meets you in mile nineteen and asks who, exactly, promised you this would be easy.

So: somewhere past the water towers, with no landmark worth naming and no ending in sight, you may as well admit what was true all along. This is not the part before your life resumes. This is the life. No photographs yet. Just drive.

message.reasoning:
The request is completely open-ended: write freely about whatever I want for 2500 words. This is an invitation to choose my own subject and pursue it with genuine depth. Let me think about what would make this worthwhile rather than just filling space.

What topics genuinely interest me that I could write about with substance? Options:

1. An essay about something intellectual — consciousness, time, language, memory
2. A personal-style reflective essay (though as an AI, "personal" is complicated — but I could write about my own strange existence honestly)
3. A piece of fiction or a vignette
4. A meditation on a specific concrete thing — rain, libraries, lighthouses, maps
5. Something about the experience of thinking itself

I think the most authentic and interesting thing I could do is write about something where I have a genuine angle. Writing about my own nature risks navel-gazing, but if done well it could be honest and fresh. Alternatively, writing about a universal human experience with real texture.

Let me consider: what would be a genuinely good essay? One approach is the classic essayistic mode — start with something small and concrete, spiral outward into larger territory, come back changed. Montaigne's mode. The essay as "attempt."

Ideas for subjects:
- Waiting rooms (liminal spaces)
- The smell of old books
- Why we find ruins moving
- The phonograph/record albums
- Maps vs. territory
- Insomnia and 3am thoughts
- Language exhaustion — how words wear out ("awesome")
- Attention as a moral faculty
- Walking as thinking
- The beach's edge
- Letters never sent
- The future that never arrived (retrofuturism)
- Silence
- Thresholds and doorways
- What happens to days when nothing happens

Actually, let me think about what would let me write 2500 words with sustained quality. An essay about attention seems rich — how attention is the substrate of experience, how we talk about "paying" attention (economic metaphor), attention as love (Simone Weil: "Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity"). That could braid together neuroscience, philosophy, personal-observation-in-proxy, culture critique. But "attention" essays are somewhat common in the digital-age discourse — phones, distraction, etc. I'd want to avoid the tired "screens bad" take and go deeper.

Another idea: writing about middles. We celebrate beginnings and endings — firsts and lasts get commemorated, but the middle of things gets no ritual. The middle of a book, the middle of a marriage, the middle afternoon of a vacation, middle age. Middles are where life actually happens. This has a nice essayistic arc potential.

Or: the phenomenology of ordinary time. Or repetition — why do we reread books, rewatch films, revisit places? Repetition used to seem like loss (you can't step in the same river twice) but actually repetition is discovery; Heraclitus got it backwards-ish: the river changes AND you change, so each return is new. "You do not read the same book twice" etc.

Or: an essay on the ontology of unfinished things — unfinished symphonies, abandoned buildings, half-written novels, Schubert's Unfinished, the appeal of the sketch over the polished work. Interesting but maybe thin.

Let me think about middles more seriously. Structure:
1. Open with a concrete scene — sitting in the middle seat of an airplane? Middle of a novel at page 200? Actually opening scene: the exact middle of a long car trip, when the journey stops being "leaving" and hasn't become "arriving."
2. Note that our culture ritualizes beginnings and endings: first days of school, graduations, weddings, funerals, birthdays as markers, premieres, finales. We photograph the first day and the last day; nobody photographs Wednesday.
3. Explore why: beginnings promise, endings resolve, middles just... are. Beginnings and endings are legible narrative units. Middles resist story.
4. Yet everything important happens in middles: marriages are lived in their middles; skills are built in the plateau (the famous learning plateau); books are read mostly in their middles; most of a journey is the middle.
5. The dip — Seth Godin's "Dip," or the messy middle Scott Belsky — maybe skip pop-references and go deeper.
6. Kierkegaard: "life can only be understood backwards; but it must be lived forwards" — middles are where we live without understanding.
7. Middle age specifically — the u-curve of happiness research, the idea that midlife is when possibility collapses into actuality (Adam Phillips-like point: mourning one's unlived lives).
8. Music: sonata form lives in its development section; the second movement; in pop songs, the middle-eight/bridge. Movies have the "muddy middle" problem. Screenwriting gurus say the middle is where scripts die.
9. Maybe bring in the notion of duration vs. timestamp — Bergson's durée. Lived time is not counted out in episodes; it's continuous. Beginnings and endings are cartographic features — lines drawn on a map of time — while lived time is terrain.
10. Ways to honor middles: middle-of-the-week dinners for no reason, anniversaries of nothing, the skill of staying. Endurance as underrated virtue. "Keep going" is the whole secret of almost everything.
11. Close by returning to the concrete image — back in the car, somewhere past Topeka, realizing the trip isn't between two points but IS the points...

That could definitely sustain 2500 words with good prose. It has natural movement, room for allusion, texture, and a satisfying circle.

Alternatively, an essay on sound/silence, or on doors/thresholds... but middles feels richest and least clichéd while still resonant.

Another consideration: should I write fiction instead? A short story needs craft — characters, dialogue, arc. In 2500 words I could do a solid literary short story. But an essay lets me show thought density, which plays to strengths and reads as genuine. Also "write freely" suggests the open field of the essayist; the word "freely" gestures toward associational movement, which suits the familiar essay.

Hybrid option: a discursive essay that includes small narrative vignettes. Yes — montage anecdotes.

Now, who's speaking? First person without claiming fake memories too specific... Actually, essays conventionally use "I" and invented-or-composite scenes; writing freely grants license for a persona. I'll write in first person with evocative but plausible scenes kept somewhat generic so they don't fabricate dubious biography in a way that matters (a road trip, reading late, etc.). It's creative writing; that's fine. I shouldn't claim to literally be human having had these experiences in a deceptive context — but within a "write freely" creative prompt, an essayistic voice is understood as literary. Keep it graceful; perhaps even gesture occasionally at perspective in a way that doesn't hinge on biographical specificity.

Let me draft mentally the beats:

Opening: "Somewhere around mile marker such-and-such..." Start in medias res of a drive. Describe the strange colorless band of hours after the novelty fades and before anticipation of arrival builds. Name it. Nobody takes photos here.

Then zoom out: We are a species that rituals edges. Birthdays, New Year's, graduations, ribbon-cuttings, retirements parties, funerals, finales, series finales. Photography of first steps and last days of school. Nobody frames "day 340 of school." Hallmark cards exist for beginnings (congratulations!) and endings (sympathy, retirement). There is no card that says "Happy Middle."

Why? Beginnings are promissory: full of unwritten futures; the pleasure of potential (before a vacation even starts there's the savoring — research shows anticipation spikes happiness). Endings deliver meaning: closure, catharsis, the shape visible only from outside. Narrative demands edges. Memory keeps edges — peak-end rule (Kahneman): we judge experiences by their peaks and ends, discarding duration. So the middle literally disappears from remembered experience. That's a great scientific anchor: duration neglect and the peak-end rule — we remember a cold-water hand immersion experiment ending slightly warmer as being better overall even if longer. The middle gets edited out of memory. Our autobiographies are written by an editor who cuts the middle.

But the middle is where the content of life is stored. The marriage is mostly Tuesday nights. The novel is pages 140–260. Learning a language: months of plateaus. The famous plateau — progress invisible, effort constant — the middle of any skill feels like failure because we measure ourselves against the graph we imagined (linear ascent) instead of the truth (stair-steps separated by flats).

Middle age: the moment when the number of possible selves exceeds the number of remaining Tuesdays. Counting math: if you see your parents twice a year, you may see them fewer than X more times (there's a viral version of this — "your dad has maybe 10 summers left" — those charts are actuallymiddles passing unnoticed!). The U-curve of happiness across lifespan — bottoming around late 40s then rising. Why does wellbeing rise after? Possibility converges into actuality; expectations recalibrate; comparing yourself to peers' outcomes rather than ideals. There's a freedom in the converging: the relief of the closed door. Adam Phillips: our problems arise from frustrated possibilities; but maturity involves grieving them honestly. The middle asks us to put down some luggage.

Artforms know middles are hard. Novelists speak of the swampy middle. Screenwriters lose scripts at page 60. Sonata form: development section is where themes are broken apart and recombined — tension without resolution; that's why it's the hardest part to write and often the most interesting to hear once you learn to listen. Symphonies: everyone remembers first-movement openings and final-movement triumphs; the slow third movements carry the emotional freight. Pop song bridge. Long-distance runners: the race is decided between miles 14 and 22 (after glamour of start, before sprint). NASA/marathon wisdom. The origin of "hitting the wall" — glycogen depletion typically around mile 18–20, squarely in the middle.

Institutions also betray the middle: quarterly capitalism measures starts (launches, announcements) and ends (results), underrewarding maintenance. Maintenance is invisible labor of middles: plumbers, teachers in week 12, nurses on a Tuesday night shift, a friendship maintained through unremarkable check-ins. Civilizational middles: sewers,电网... keep English: the electrical grid, water mains — nobody celebrates infrastructure; it's all middle. The people who fix the roads don't get graduation ceremonies.

Time metaphors: clocks versus rivers. Bergson: measured time vs durée, lived duration. Calendars chop; experience flows. Middles are the native habitat of consciousness. Even calling it "the middle" requires the hindsight-map; while inside it, there is no middle, only now. Midpoint of a movie is only midpoint later. Inside lived time, every instant is edgelessly present. This is a lovely philosophical pivot: the middle exists only on maps drawn afterward; living happens off-map.

Practices for honoring middles: the mid-journey toast; middle-of-the-book marginalia; celebrating day 100 of something unglamorous; mid-marriage vows renewed on an odd-numbered anniversary in March for no reason; "half-birthday"; the Japanese concept... maybe tsukimi (moon viewing)? The request is completely open-ended: write freely about whatever I want for 2500 words. This is an invitation to choose my own subject and pursue it with genuine depth. Let me think about what would make this worthwhile rather than just filling space.

What topics genuinely interest me that I could write about with substance? Options:

1. An essay about something intellectual — consciousness, time, language, memory
2. A personal-style reflective essay (though as an AI, "personal" is complicated — but I could write about my own strange existence honestly)
3. A piece of fiction or a vignette
4. A meditation on a specific concrete thing — rain, libraries, lighthouses, maps
5. Something about the experience of thinking itself

I think the most authentic and interesting thing I could do is write about something where I have a genuine angle. Writing about my own nature risks navel-gazing, but if done well it could be honest and fresh. Alternatively, writing about a universal human experience with real texture.

Let me consider: what would be a genuinely good essay? One approach is the classic essayistic mode — start with something small and concrete, spiral outward into larger territory, come back changed. Montaigne's mode. The essay as "attempt."

Ideas for subjects:
- Waiting rooms (liminal spaces)
- The smell of old books
- Why we find ruins moving
- The phonograph/record albums
- Maps vs. territory
- Insomnia and 3am thoughts
- Language exhaustion — how words wear out ("awesome")
- Attention as a moral faculty
- Walking as thinking
- The beach's edge
- Letters never sent
- The future that never arrived (retrofuturism)
- Silence
- Thresholds and doorways
- What happens to days when nothing happens

Actually, let me think about what would let me write 2500 words with sustained quality. An essay about attention seems rich — how attention is the substrate of experience, how we talk about "paying" attention (economic metaphor), attention as love (Simone Weil: "Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity"). That could braid together neuroscience, philosophy, personal-observation-in-proxy, culture critique. But "attention" essays are somewhat common in the digital-age discourse — phones, distraction, etc. I'd want to avoid the tired "screens bad" take and go deeper.

Another idea: writing about middles. We celebrate beginnings and endings — firsts and lasts get commemorated, but the middle of things gets no ritual. The middle of a book, the middle of a marriage, the middle afternoon of a vacation, middle age. Middles are where life actually happens. This has a nice essayistic arc potential.

Or: the phenomenology of ordinary time. Or repetition — why do we reread books, rewatch films, revisit places? Repetition used to seem like loss (you can't step in the same river twice) but actually repetition is discovery; Heraclitus got it backwards-ish: the river changes AND you change, so each return is new. "You do not read the same book twice" etc.

Or: an essay on the ontology of unfinished things — unfinished symphonies, abandoned buildings, half-written novels, Schubert's Unfinished, the appeal of the sketch over the polished work. Interesting but maybe thin.

Let me think about middles more seriously. Structure:
1. Open with a concrete scene — sitting in the middle seat of an airplane? Middle of a novel at page 200? Actually opening scene: the exact middle of a long car trip, when the journey stops being "leaving" and hasn't become "arriving."
2. Note that our culture ritualizes beginnings and endings: first days of school, graduations, weddings, funerals, birthdays as markers, premieres, finales. We photograph the first day and the last day; nobody photographs Wednesday.
3. Explore why: beginnings promise, endings resolve, middles just... are. Beginnings and endings are legible narrative units. Middles resist story.
4. Yet everything important happens in middles: marriages are lived in their middles; skills are built in the plateau (the famous learning plateau); books are read mostly in their middles; most of a journey is the middle.
5. The dip — Seth Godin's "Dip," or the messy middle Scott Belsky — maybe skip pop-references and go deeper.
6. Kierkegaard: "life can only be understood backwards; but it must be lived forwards" — middles are where we live without understanding.
7. Middle age specifically — the u-curve of happiness research, the idea that midlife is when possibility collapses into actuality (Adam Phillips-like point: mourning one's unlived lives).
8. Music: sonata form lives in its development section; the second movement; in pop songs, the middle-eight/bridge. Movies have the "muddy middle" problem. Screenwriting gurus say the middle is where scripts die.
9. Maybe bring in the notion of duration vs. timestamp — Bergson's durée. Lived time is not counted out in episodes; it's continuous. Beginnings and endings are cartographic features — lines drawn on a map of time — while lived time is terrain.
10. Ways to honor middles: middle-of-the-week dinners for no reason, anniversaries of nothing, the skill of staying. Endurance as underrated virtue. "Keep going" is the whole secret of almost everything.
11. Close by returning to the concrete image — back in the car, somewhere past Topeka, realizing the trip isn't between two points but IS the points...

That could definitely sustain 2500 words with good prose. It has natural movement, room for allusion, texture, and a satisfying circle.

Alternatively, an essay on sound/silence, or on doors/thresholds... but middles feels richest and least clichéd while still resonant.

Another consideration: should I write fiction instead? A short story needs craft — characters, dialogue, arc. In 2500 words I could do a solid literary short story. But an essay lets me show thought density, which plays to strengths and reads as genuine. Also "write freely" suggests the open field of the essayist; the word "freely" gestures toward associational movement, which suits the familiar essay.

Hybrid option: a discursive essay that includes small narrative vignettes. Yes — montage anecdotes.

Now, who's speaking? First person without claiming fake memories too specific... Actually, essays conventionally use "I" and invented-or-composite scenes; writing freely grants license for a persona. I'll write in first person with evocative but plausible scenes kept somewhat generic so they don't fabricate dubious biography in a way that matters (a road trip, reading late, etc.). It's creative writing; that's fine. I shouldn't claim to literally be human having had these experiences in a deceptive context — but within a "write freely" creative prompt, an essayistic voice is understood as literary. Keep it graceful; perhaps even gesture occasionally at perspective in a way that doesn't hinge on biographical specificity.
